live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card skimmers that hide in online checkout pages
next.in_short: MageCart is the name for web skimming that steals card details at checkout. Reports describe many groups, hits on big retailers and supply-chain attacks, and campaigns that ran for years.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card data from compromised eCommerce websites.
WIRED describes Magecart as a group of hackers that steals credit card numbers, often by skimming card data from ecommerce sites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups use the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Headlines in Malpedia's reference list name several sub-groups, including Magecart Group 4, Group 8, Group 12, Keeper and ATMZOW.
Malpedia's reference headlines mention campaigns hitting online ordering platforms and restaurants, and campus online stores in the US and Canada.
Trend Micro cites Newegg, Target, Home Depot and Ticketmaster as examples, and says no website is safe from skimming attacks.

ANY.RUN says victims of one campaign were mostly retail e-commerce sites, in at least 12 countries and concentrated in Spain, France and the United States. It says banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
According to Malpedia, the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It relays card data to command-and-control servers.

Trend Micro lists three tactics: infecting third-party companies that supply code to other sites, scanning the internet for unsecured servers, and writing skimming code that works across many payment pages.
RiskIQ reports that on Newegg the skimmer sat on the payment page itself, not in a separate script. It says the code was recognisable from the British Airways incident.
Malwarebytes found skimmers hosted on Heroku. They overlaid a rogue iframe on the payment form and sent stolen data back in encoded form.
ANY.RUN describes checkout hijacking, imitation of payment pages, heavily obfuscated JavaScript and card data sent over WebSocket.
Sucuri says the ATMZOW skimmer is planted through Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 its operators registered 40 new domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
RiskIQ reports that the Newegg skimmer became active around August 14th, 2018, and was removed on September 18th. Customers were exposed for over a month.
In July 2019, WIRED said the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months, helped by poor security hygiene.
A report on the October 2019 Volusion breach says more than 6,500 stores were impacted, and the number could be higher. It calls the incident a Magecart-style supply-chain attack.
The same report says seven service providers were breached in May 2019 through misconfigured cloud-hosting accounts.
Sucuri says Google removed one Tag Manager container, but the ATMZOW actors created new containers and reinfected sites.
ANY.RUN reports a Magecart-style campaign active for at least 24 months and supported by over 100 domains.
Store owners should review which scripts their checkout pages load and treat unexpected ones as a sign of compromise.
Shoppers should watch their card statements for charges they do not recognise.
